steps.title: Every Formula Starts with =

blocks.text: In your QuickDeliver Orders sheet, most cells hold plain values — an amount, a city, a date. A formula changes that: it tells Excel to compute a result instead. Every formula begins with the equal sign (=). Without it, Excel treats the entry as text.

Excel's four arithmetic operators are + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), and / (division). You can combine them with literal numbers or cell addresses: =D3-D2 subtracts one order's amount from another; =D2*2 doubles it. To reference another cell, type its address after the = and operator.

Built-in functions follow the same = prefix but add a name and parentheses: =SUM(D2:D21) totals every amount in that range of your Orders sheet. Type =, the function name, an opening parenthesis, select the range, close the parenthesis, then press Enter. The cell shows the computed result.

steps.lede: A formula turns a cell into a calculator — here's the pattern every formula follows.

segments.label: Formulas always start with =, and the four core arithmetic operators
segments.summary: The presenter distinguishes a formula (any expression starting with =) from a function (a built-in tool that can appear inside a formula). Omitting the = sign causes Excel to treat the entry as text rather than a calculation. The arithmetic operators are then demonstrated one by one: + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division, each with a concrete numeric example that shows the result Excel returns.

segments.label: Starting a formula with = and calling a built-in function over a selected range
segments.summary: The presenter types = in a cell to begin a formula, then types a function name (MAX), presses Tab to accept it, and drags to select a range of cells as the argument. The closing parenthesis is added and Enter is pressed to confirm. The same steps are repeated with MIN on the same range, showing how the function-call pattern — equal sign, name, opening parenthesis, range, closing parenthesis, Enter — applies to any built-in function.

blocks.group_title: Entering formulas: the equal sign, arithmetic operators, and function calls

bridge.before: Watch how = signals a formula and how each operator or function name follows it directly. The first clip uses plain numbers; the second shows a range argument inside parentheses.
bridge.after: These clips cover f1–f3 but leave out cell-to-cell formulas (f4) and operator precedence (f5); the teaching text covers both fully.

steps.title: Operator Precedence and Parentheses

blocks.text: Excel evaluates multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. =5+2*3 gives 11, not 21. Wrap the addition in parentheses — =(5+2)*3 — to get 21. Whenever a formula mixes operators, check the order or add parentheses to be explicit.

steps.lede: Multiplication runs before addition — unless you use parentheses.

steps.title: The Required Formula Prefix
steps.lede: Which character must every Excel formula begin with?

public.prompt:
You type the following into cell D4 of the Orders sheet: D2+D3

What happens when you press Enter?

options.text: Excel treats it as text and displays the string "D2+D3" in the cell.
Excel adds the values in D2 and D3 and shows the numeric result.
Excel shows a #NAME? error because the cell addresses are invalid.
Excel shows a #VALUE! error because + requires numbers.

opt_b.message: Without a leading = Excel does not evaluate the entry as a formula. It stores the literal text "D2+D3" instead of computing a sum.

opt_c.message: #NAME? appears when Excel cannot recognise a name inside a formula. Here there is no formula at all — the entry has no = prefix, so Excel stores it as plain text.

opt_d.message: #VALUE! occurs when a formula receives the wrong type of argument. But without a leading = there is no formula to evaluate, so no error is raised — the entry is stored as text.

correct.message: Correct! Without the = prefix Excel treats the entry as plain text and displays "D2+D3" literally. Every formula must start with = to tell Excel to compute a value.

incorrect.message: Formulas in Excel always begin with the equal sign (=). Without it, Excel treats the entry as plain text and displays it as-is, not as a computed result.

hints: Think about what tells Excel that an entry is a formula rather than a label.
Try typing just the letter A in a cell — Excel shows 'A', not an error.

steps.title: Writing a Function Formula
steps.lede: Which formula correctly sums the range C2:C21 on the Orders sheet?

public.prompt:
Which formula correctly sums the range D2:D21 on the Orders sheet?

The Orders sheet has 20 rows of data in rows 2–21. You want to add up all the values in the amount column (D2:D21) using the SUM function. Which formula is correctly structured?

opt_b.message: This is missing the = prefix. Without it, Excel stores the entry as text rather than evaluating the SUM function.

opt_c.message: The parentheses are required. The correct syntax is =SUM(range) — the opening parenthesis immediately follows the function name, and the range goes inside.

opt_d.message: =SUM(D2,D21) adds only two individual cells: D2 and D21. To sum a continuous range of cells, use the colon notation: D2:D21.

correct.message: Correct! =SUM(D2:D21) follows the required structure: = prefix, function name, opening parenthesis, the range D2:D21, closing parenthesis. This sums all 20 amount values.

incorrect.message: A function formula needs: = prefix, the function name, an opening parenthesis, the range argument, and a closing parenthesis — for example =SUM(D2:D21).

hints: Every formula starts with =. Then comes the function name, then the range inside parentheses.
D2:D21 uses a colon to mean 'from D2 to D21'. A comma would list only two separate cells.

steps.title: Write Formulas on the Orders Sheet
steps.lede: Apply arithmetic operators, cell references, and a function call to the QuickDeliver data.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has order amounts in column D (rows 2–21). Row 2 (LG-2001) has amount **4500** and row 3 (LG-2002) has amount **7200**.

**Task 1 — subtraction:** In cell E1, write a formula that subtracts the amount in D2 from the amount in D3 (D3 minus D2). The result should be **2700**.

**Task 2 — operator precedence:** In cell E2, write a formula that first adds D2 and D3, then multiplies the sum by 2. Use parentheses to force the addition before the multiplication. The result should be **23400**.

tests.message_on_fail: E1 should equal 2700 (D3 minus D2 = 7200 - 4500). Make sure your formula starts with = and uses the - operator between D3 and D2.
E2 should equal 23400 ((D2+D3)*2 = (4500+7200)*2 = 11700*2). Without parentheses, =D2+D3*2 gives 18600 because * is evaluated before +. Wrap the addition in parentheses: =(D2+D3)*2.

correct.message: Well done! E1 uses = and the - operator to subtract D2 from D3, returning 2700. E2 uses parentheses to force the addition (D2+D3) before the multiplication by 2, returning 23400. Without parentheses, =D2+D3*2 would give 18600 because * has higher precedence than +.

incorrect.message: Check both cells. E1 needs =D3-D2 (the = prefix, then D3, then -, then D2). E2 needs parentheses around the addition: =(D2+D3)*2. Without parentheses, multiplication happens before addition and the result is wrong.

hints: Every formula must start with =. Without it, Excel stores the entry as text.
Parentheses change the order of operations: =(D2+D3)*2 adds first, then multiplies.

steps.title: Relative and Absolute References

blocks.text: A relative reference such as D2 is position-based: copy the formula one row down and D2 becomes D3 automatically. By default, every new formula uses relative references. This is what you want when each row should calculate against its own data.

An absolute reference such as $H$1 always points to the same cell, no matter where you copy the formula. Dollar signs lock both the column letter and the row number. If a delivery fee rate lives in H1, =D2*$H$1 copied down every order row keeps pointing to H1 for the rate while D2 shifts to D3, D4, and so on.

blocks.change_summary: After copying H2 down to H3 and H4, the relative part (D2→D3→D4) adjusts while the absolute part ($H$1) stays fixed.

steps.lede: Copy a formula down a column and watch which parts shift — and which stay fixed.

segments.label: Relative, absolute, and mixed references demonstrated by copying formulas across a sheet
segments.summary: The instructor starts with a simple formula that multiplies a value by 2, then copies it to show how the cell address shifts automatically to match the new position — this is relative referencing. Next, dollar signs are added before both the column letter and row number to lock the address completely, so the formula always points to the same cell no matter where it is pasted — absolute referencing. A clinic appointment tracker then reinforces relative references by copying a set of formulas across a full week of data with no manual edits. Finally, a sales-bonus grid introduces mixed referencing: the column is locked with a dollar sign so the formula always reads from the sales-amount column, while the row is locked separately so it always reads from the chosen bonus-rate row, letting a single formula fill every combination in the grid correctly.

blocks.group_title: Reference lock in action: watching a cell address shift — or stay fixed — as a formula is copied

bridge.before: Watch how the address in the formula bar changes — or doesn't — each time the formula is pasted to a new cell. The clip uses 'lock' as a synonym for absolute reference.
bridge.after: The clip covers all three reference types. Devspace's text adds the tax-rate column example and clarifies that relative referencing is the spreadsheet default.

steps.title: Mixed References: Lock One Dimension

blocks.text: A mixed reference locks only one dimension. $A1 locks the column (A stays, row shifts); A$1 locks the row (1 stays, column shifts). Use a mixed reference when copying a formula across both rows and columns and only one axis should stay fixed.

steps.lede: Lock just the column or just the row — not both.

steps.title: Constructing a Mixed Reference
steps.lede: Which reference locks the column but lets the row shift when copied down?

public.prompt:
You are building a multiplication table. Row 1 holds the column multipliers (B1, C1, D1, …) and column A holds the row multipliers (A2, A3, A4, …). You want to enter one formula in B2 and copy it across the entire table so that it always multiplies the correct row multiplier by the correct column multiplier.

Which formula should you enter in B2?

opt_b.message: $A$2 locks both the column and the row of the row multiplier. When you copy the formula down, the row part ($2) never changes, so every row in the table uses A2 instead of A3, A4, etc.

opt_c.message: =A2*B1 uses fully relative references. When copied across columns, A2 shifts to B2, C2, etc., so the formula no longer reads from column A. When copied down, B1 shifts to B2, B3, etc., losing the header row.

opt_d.message: $A$2 locks both dimensions of the row multiplier, so copying down always reads A2 instead of A3, A4, etc. You need $A2 (lock column A, let the row adjust) to keep the row multiplier in column A while allowing the row to change.

correct.message: Correct! =$A2*B$1 uses two mixed references. $A2 locks column A so the row multiplier always comes from column A, while the row number adjusts as you copy down. B$1 locks row 1 so the column multiplier always comes from row 1, while the column letter adjusts as you copy across.

incorrect.message: A mixed reference locks one dimension and lets the other adjust. $A2 locks the column (A stays fixed) but lets the row change when copied down. B$1 locks the row (1 stays fixed) but lets the column change when copied across. Together, =$A2*B$1 fills the entire multiplication table correctly from one formula.

hints: The $ sign locks the part that follows it: $A locks the column, $1 locks the row.
Ask yourself: when I copy this formula down, which part must NOT change? When I copy across, which part must NOT change?

steps.title: Apply Reference Types to the Orders Sheet
steps.lede: Choose the right reference type for each copy scenario.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has order amounts in column D (rows 2–4). Cell H1 holds the tax rate **0.075** (7.5%).

**Task:** In cells E2, E3, and E4, write a formula that multiplies each row's amount (D2, D3, D4) by the shared tax rate in H1. Use an **absolute reference** for H1 so the tax-rate address does not change when the formula is copied down. Use a **relative reference** for the amount cell so it adjusts to the correct row.

- E2 should equal **337.5** (4500 × 0.075)
- E3 should equal **540** (7200 × 0.075)
- E4 should equal **232.5** (3100 × 0.075)

tests.message_on_fail: E2 should equal 337.5 (D2 × H1 = 4500 × 0.075). Use =D2*$H$1 — the $ signs lock H1 so it does not shift when copied.
E3 should equal 540 (D3 × H1 = 7200 × 0.075). If you copied =D2*$H$1 down, D2 should have adjusted to D3 while $H$1 stayed fixed.
E4 should equal 232.5 (D4 × H1 = 3100 × 0.075). Check that E4 uses D4 (relative, adjusts per row) and $H$1 (absolute, stays fixed).

correct.message: Excellent! =D2*$H$1 uses a relative reference for D2 (it adjusts to D3, D4 as you copy down) and an absolute reference for $H$1 (the $ signs lock both the column H and row 1, so the tax-rate cell never shifts). This is the key pattern for applying a shared rate to a column of values.

incorrect.message: Use =D2*$H$1 in E2. The $ signs in $H$1 lock the tax-rate cell so it does not shift when the formula is copied. D2 has no $ signs, so it adjusts to D3 in E3 and D4 in E4. If you used =D2*H1 (no $), H1 would shift to H2, H3, etc. when copied down.

hints: Add $ before both the column letter and the row number of H1 to lock it: $H$1.
Leave D2 without $ signs so it automatically becomes D3 when you copy the formula to E3.

steps.title: Formulas and Reference Types — Key Takeaways

blocks.text: Every formula starts with =, combines cell references and operators or a function call, and follows Excel's precedence rules unless parentheses override them. Relative references shift when copied; absolute references ($A$1) stay fixed; mixed references lock one dimension. That combination is the basis for every calculation you'll write in a spreadsheet.

blocks.title: Up Next: Aggregation Functions
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll use SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA to summarise the entire Orders column in a single formula.

Excel distinguishes a formula from plain text by the leading = sign. Type 5+2 and Excel stores the text '5+2'. Type =5+2 and Excel computes 7. Every formula — whether it uses arithmetic operators or a function like SUM — must start with =.

A function formula follows the pattern =NAME(range). =SUM(D2:D21) is correct: equal sign, function name, opening parenthesis, the range, closing parenthesis. Omitting the = or the parentheses produces an error or plain text, not a computed result.

A mixed reference uses exactly one $ sign. $A1 locks the column letter A — copy the formula across columns and A never changes, but the row number shifts. A$1 locks the row number 1 — copy down rows and 1 never changes, but the column shifts. Two $ signs ($A$1) lock both and make the reference fully absolute.
